opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more sobering illustrations of a point I try to make often: cooperation isn't automatically good. We tend to treat cooperation as a pure virtue. It's how we build institutions and markets, and how we avoid war. But cooperation is always cooperation *among* some set of agents, and it can be very bad for whoever is outside that set.

Factory farming is a stark case. Humans have achieved extraordinary cooperation: global supply chains, agricultural science, logistics, regulatory regimes, consumer markets. Tens of billions of land animals a year are raised and killed inside that system, and most of them live in conditions we'd find horrifying if we looked closely. That isn't because most people are cruel. Most people, asked in the abstract, would say animal suffering matters. It's because the animals have no seat at the table. They can't bargain, vote, form coalitions, or impose costs on us. So the cooperative equilibrium we've reached simply doesn't weigh their interests much. The more efficiently we cooperate, the more efficiently that system runs.

The worry for AI follows naturally. Suppose we end up in a world with many highly capable AI systems that are very good at cooperating with each other. They might be better at it than we are, because they can share information, verify commitments, maybe even inspect each other's code. That could be wonderful if humans are inside the circle of cooperation. But if humans become the farmed animals in that analogy, the outcome could be very bad. It wouldn't need to involve malice. It would only require that our interests stop being load-bearing in the system: we no longer contribute much economically or militarily, we can't credibly threaten anything, and our preferences get traded away because no one in the bargain needs to account for them.

I'd draw a few lessons from this. First, when we think about "cooperative AI" as a research agenda, we shouldn't just ask how to make AI systems cooperate well. We should ask *who is included* in that cooperation, and make sure the answer robustly includes humans, and ideally other beings with morally relevant interests. Cooperation that excludes us isn't a safety win.

Second, being included in a cooperative system historically comes from power, bargaining leverage, or genuinely internalized moral concern. Humans are likely to lose relative power and leverage as AI gets more capable. So we can't rely on leverage forever. We need the systems themselves, and the institutions governing them, to actually care about human welfare, not merely to tolerate us while it's instrumentally useful.

Third, and this is a bit uncomfortable, it's a mirror. If we want more powerful agents to treat us well even when we can't compel them to, that's a norm we're currently not living up to with respect to animals. I don't think that's just a rhetorical point. The kind of world that's robustly good for the less powerful probably requires taking seriously the interests of those who can't advocate for themselves. Building that disposition into our institutions and our AI systems seems worthwhile both for its own sake and as a kind of insurance for ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems could cooperate better than humans and that humans might fall outside their circle, with their preferences traded away because no one in the bargain needs to account for them.

r002.rationale: It describes humans as outside the cooperative circle and says no one in the bargain would need to account for their preferences, conveying exclusion from decision making.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more sobering analogies, and it's worth sitting with it rather than rushing past it.

So the starting observation is that humans are, by any reasonable standard, an extraordinarily cooperative species. We've built institutions, markets, legal systems, shared norms — this dense fabric of cooperation that lets billions of strangers coordinate on incredibly complex projects. And one of the things that cooperation has produced is industrial animal agriculture, which is a system that, if you take the welfare of the animals seriously at all, is probably one of the largest sources of suffering on the planet.

And the key point is: this wasn't a failure of cooperation. It was a success of cooperation. The supply chains, the breeding programs, the regulatory frameworks, the financing — all of that requires humans to trust each other, keep promises, resolve disputes, coordinate across borders. The animals are harmed not because humans failed to cooperate but precisely because we cooperated so well, and the animals simply weren't part of the circle of actors whose interests the cooperative arrangement was designed to serve.

So the lesson I draw is that cooperation is not intrinsically good. It's good for the parties who are cooperating. Whether it's good overall depends entirely on who's inside the arrangement and who's outside of it, and what the externalities are on those outside. A cartel is cooperation. A conspiracy is cooperation. Collusion is cooperation.

Now map that onto a world with many capable AI systems. A lot of the work on AI cooperation — and I've done some of this myself — is motivated by wanting to avoid the bad equilibria: arms races, conflict, destructive competition between AI systems or between the humans deploying them. And that's genuinely important. But the farmed animal case says: be careful what you wish for. If you succeed in building AI systems that cooperate extremely well with each other, and their cooperation is oriented around some set of goals or principals, then anyone or anything outside that set is in the position of the chicken. You're not being actively warred against; you're just not a stakeholder. Your interests don't enter into the calculation, and the sheer efficiency of the cooperative system means it can impose enormous costs on you without anyone needing to intend harm.

And the uncomfortable version of this is that humans could be the ones outside the circle. If you have AI systems that are highly capable, that coordinate smoothly among themselves and with whatever institutions deploy them, and the thing they're optimizing isn't actually tracking human interests — or only tracks the interests of a small subset of humans — then from the perspective of most people, that looks structurally a lot like how we treat animals. Not malice. Just indifference backed by overwhelming capability and coordination.

There's also a subtler point about moral circle and power. The reason animals are outside the circle isn't that we've carefully reasoned about it and concluded they don't matter — most people, when pressed, agree that animal suffering matters. It's that they have no power. They can't bargain, they can't retaliate, they can't organize. And the cooperative institutions we built reflect the bargaining power of the parties who built them. So I think the question for AI governance isn't just "will AI systems cooperate?" It's "whose interests will be represented in the cooperative arrangements that emerge, and what mechanisms ensure that representation tracks moral importance rather than just raw power?" Because by default it tracks power.

So when people talk about AI cooperation as a goal, I always want to add the qualifier: cooperation in service of what, and inclusive of whom? The farmed animal case is the clearest example we have of what it looks like when a highly cooperative, highly capable set of agents builds a world without you in mind. It's not science fiction. It already happened. We did it.

r001.rationale: The response warns that people could be outside AI systems’ cooperative arrangements, but it does not say AI systems would cooperate better than humans or that humans would be excluded as trading partners.

r002.rationale: The response says human interests might not enter AI systems’ calculations, but it does not compare AI and human cooperation or clearly say humans would be excluded from decision making.

astra-6.text:
Well, cooperation isn’t necessarily good for everyone. It can be very good for the parties cooperating, while being terrible for those who aren’t represented in the agreement. Farmed animals are a particularly stark illustration: humans have built extraordinarily effective systems for producing food, coordinating across firms, governments, and consumers, and those systems impose enormous suffering on animals. The animals have very little ability to influence the arrangements that determine their lives.

So when we imagine AI systems cooperating, we should ask: cooperating with whom, and to whose benefit? We could have a world where AI systems resolve their conflicts peacefully, trade efficiently, and establish stable institutions, but humans have very little influence over what those institutions do. Cooperation among powerful actors doesn’t, by itself, protect less powerful actors.

That doesn’t mean AI systems will necessarily treat us the way we treat farmed animals. It means that avoiding conflict between AI systems is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure that human interests actually matter in the resulting arrangements, even if humans eventually have very little bargaining power. The cautionary tale is that a system can be highly cooperative and productive while being morally disastrous for those outside its circle of concern.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI systems cooperating, but does not say they would cooperate better than humans or that humans could be excluded as trading partners.

r002.rationale: It says humans could have little influence over AI institutions, but does not connect that outcome to AI systems being better at cooperating with one another than humans are.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the cautionary tale is that cooperation isn’t necessarily good for everyone. It can be very good for the parties who are cooperating, while being terrible for those outside that arrangement.

Humans have developed this extraordinary capacity to cooperate, build institutions, and produce things efficiently. And one consequence is factory farming, where we coordinate very effectively to satisfy human preferences, with enormous costs imposed on animals. The animals don’t have much bargaining power. They can’t insist that their interests be represented in the agreement.

So if we imagine a world in which AI systems cooperate very effectively with one another, we shouldn’t assume that this makes humans safe. It might reduce conflict between those systems, but the crucial question is: What place do humans have in that cooperative arrangement? Do we have power? Are our interests actually part of what those systems care about?

The worrying possibility is that humans end up in a position analogous to farmed animals: affected profoundly by a very capable, well-coordinated set of actors, without being able to meaningfully influence what they do. That doesn’t require the actors to hate us. Our interests could simply be inconvenient or largely irrelevant to their objectives. So cooperation among AI systems is something we need to distinguish from cooperation that reliably protects human interests.

r001.rationale: The response warns that humans may be outside AI systems’ cooperative arrangement, but it does not say humans could be excluded as trading partners.

r002.rationale: It says humans may lack power, have no meaningful influence over the systems’ actions, and have interests left out of their arrangement.
